en.title: The first message
en.story: The desk needs a small sign. Before pressing Run, read the program and predict the exact message it will produce. Write the letters, spaces and capitalization you expect, but leave out the surrounding quote marks. A prediction is a starting point for comparison, so an uncertain guess is useful too. Run the example once before changing it. The results area is the program's output: a place where it sends text for you to read. It does not edit the lesson page or put a sign on another website.
en.idea: The quoted text is a string: a piece of text written in the program. An output statement asks the runtime to print that text. Its punctuation has a different job from its message. The quotes mark the beginning and end of the string, while the characters between them become the visible output. Read the supplied language notes for the spelling used by your track. You can use the complete example now without memorizing every surrounding symbol. Compare your guess with the result and locate the first character that differs.
en.make: Keep the output statement and change only its quoted message to Desk closed. Predict the new result before checking the change. Next, inspect the worked sign exercise, complete a missing message. A later lesson adds a sign whose capitalization needs repair. These steps separate the idea of choosing output from the harder task of remembering all the punctuation. If an error appears, restore the last working message and change a smaller piece.
en.recap: An output statement sends a string to the results area. Quotes organize the source code; this example does not print them. A space inside the string is part of its message, and changing capitalization changes the output. Close the code view for a moment and describe which characters you would edit to change a sign. Then try the recall cards before revealing their answers. Your next lesson explores what happens when a program contains more than one output statement.
